subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In intaglio printmaking, where does the ink sit to create the printed image?
options: In the incised lines and recesses below the surface
On the raised surface of the block
On a flat stone treated chemically
questions.explain: Intaglio prints from ink held in lines incised or bitten below the plate surface, which is then wiped clean on top before printing under pressure.

questions.q: Colours that sit next to each other on the colour wheel, such as blue, blue-green and green, are described as:
questions.explain: Analogous colours are neighbours on the wheel and produce harmonious, low-contrast schemes.

questions.q: Impressionism, exemplified by Claude Monet, is chiefly concerned with:
options: Capturing the fleeting effects of light, atmosphere and colour
Precise academic detail and historical narrative
questions.explain: Impressionists such as Monet painted the transient effects of light and atmosphere, often outdoors with loose, visible brushwork.

questions.q: Which printmaking process is described as a 'relief' technique?
questions.explain: In a linocut the non-printing areas are cut away and ink is rolled onto the remaining raised surface, making it a relief process.

questions.q: Installation art is best defined as:
options: A three-dimensional work designed to transform the perception of a whole space
questions.explain: Installation art is created for and often fills a specific space, immersing the viewer rather than presenting a discrete object.

questions.q: A wider aperture (a lower f-number such as f/2.8) produces:
questions.explain: A wider aperture lets in more light and produces a shallower depth of field, throwing backgrounds out of focus.

questions.q: In the critical study of art, 'iconography' is the study of:
options: The subject matter, symbols and their meanings within an image
The price history of the work
questions.explain: Iconography interprets the symbols, motifs and subject matter and the meanings they carry.

questions.q: In print production, 'bleed' refers to:
options: Artwork extended beyond the trim edge so no white shows after cutting
questions.explain: Bleed is the area of artwork extended past the trim line so that, after trimming, the colour reaches the very edge of the page.

questions.q: The painting technique of building up thin, transparent layers to modify the colour beneath is called:
questions.explain: Glazing applies translucent layers over a dried underlayer, allowing light to pass through and enrich the colour.

questions.q: Georges Seurat's technique of applying small distinct dots of colour that blend in the viewer's eye is known as:
questions.explain: Pointillism (or divisionism) builds an image from tiny dots of pure colour that optically mix at a distance.

questions.q: In three-dimensional design, which process shapes thermoplastic sheet by heating it and drawing it over a mould?
questions.explain: Vacuum forming heats a plastic sheet until pliable and uses suction to pull it tightly over a mould.

questions.q: Which colour model is used for full-colour commercial process printing?
questions.explain: Process printing uses CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow and key/black) inks combined to reproduce a wide colour range.

questions.q: In the A-level investigative process, 'refining' work refers to:
options: Developing and improving ideas through experimentation and review
Starting an entirely new unrelated project
questions.explain: Refining is the ongoing development, reviewing and improving of ideas and techniques towards a resolved outcome.

questions.q: In typography, 'kerning' refers to adjusting:
options: The line spacing of a paragraph
The space between specific pairs of letters
questions.explain: Kerning is the adjustment of spacing between individual letter pairs to improve visual evenness.

questions.q: A fast shutter speed (e.g. 1/1000s) is primarily used to:
questions.explain: A fast shutter speed exposes the sensor briefly and freezes rapid movement without motion blur.

questions.q: In a formal analysis of an artwork, you would primarily discuss:
options: Line, shape, colour, tone, texture, form and composition
questions.explain: Formal analysis examines the visual elements and how they are organised, independent of subject or context.

questions.q: When analysing the 'context' of an artwork, a student should consider:
options: The social, historical, cultural or personal circumstances of its making
questions.explain: Contextual analysis situates the work within its social, historical, cultural and biographical circumstances.

questions.q: In the photographic exposure triangle, which three settings together control exposure?
options: Shutter speed, white balance and contrast
questions.explain: Exposure is governed by aperture (amount of light), shutter speed (duration) and ISO (sensor/film sensitivity).

questions.q: The Renaissance development of linear perspective allowed artists to:
options: Create a convincing illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface
questions.explain: Linear perspective, codified by Brunelleschi and Alberti, used converging lines to a vanishing point to suggest depth.

questions.q: A 'mixed-media' approach in a sketchbook investigation means:
options: Combining two or more different media in one piece
questions.explain: Mixed media combines different materials, such as collage, paint, ink and print, within a single work.

questions.q: The Bauhaus, founded in Germany in 1919, was influential mainly as a school that:
options: United art, craft, design and technology for the modern age
questions.explain: The Bauhaus integrated fine art, craft, design and industry, shaping modernist design, architecture and education.

questions.q: In typography, the small finishing strokes at the ends of letters are called:
questions.explain: Serifs are the small terminal strokes; typefaces without them are described as sans-serif.

questions.q: Abstract Expressionism's 'action painting', exemplified by Jackson Pollock, emphasised:
options: The gestural, physical act of applying paint
questions.explain: Action painting foregrounded spontaneous, energetic gesture, as in Pollock's poured and dripped canvases.

questions.q: Which artist is most strongly associated with Post-Impressionism and thickly applied, expressive brushwork in works like 'The Starry Night'?
questions.explain: Vincent van Gogh, a Post-Impressionist, is renowned for emotionally charged colour and swirling impasto brushwork.

questions.q: The lost-wax method is a traditional process for:
questions.explain: In lost-wax (cire perdue) casting a wax model is encased, melted out and replaced with molten metal.

questions.q: The Dada movement, emerging during the First World War, is best described as:
options: An anti-art response rejecting reason and bourgeois values
questions.explain: Dada was a nihilistic, anti-art reaction to the war, embracing absurdity, chance and provocation.

questions.q: Lithography is a planographic process that relies on which fundamental principle?
options: Ink held in deeply bitten grooves
Oil and water repelling one another
Pressure forcing ink through a stencil
questions.explain: Lithography exploits the mutual repulsion of grease and water so the greasy drawn image accepts ink while the dampened blank areas reject it.

questions.q: Raising the ISO setting on a camera tends to:
options: Increase sensitivity to light but add noise/grain
questions.explain: A higher ISO increases the sensor's sensitivity, allowing shooting in low light but introducing more noise or grain.

questions.q: Which assessment objective focuses on 'recording ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions'?
questions.explain: Recording covers the gathering of ideas, observations and insights relevant to the candidate's intentions, including drawing and other means.

questions.q: In screen printing, the image is created by:
options: Cutting away the background of a block
Incising lines into a metal plate
Pushing ink through open areas of a stencil on a mesh
Drawing with greasy crayon onto limestone
questions.explain: Screen printing (serigraphy) forces ink through the open mesh of a stencilled screen onto the surface below.
